newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: N.Korean defector asks: Am I the only mad person?.
newsitem.headline: N.Korean defector asks: Am I the only mad person?.

text.p: In a letter released by South Korea on Thursday, a top-ranking North Korean defector revealed the agony of his decision to flee a starving nation that he said had gone mad.
"I tormented and tormented over this," Hwang Jang-yop said in the signed note written from a South Korean embassy compound in Beijing where he is seeking asylum.

"Starting with my family, people will judge that I'm mad. But the question is: am I the only mad person?" Hwang attacked those in the North who continued to treat South Korea as the enemy and talked of turning it into a "sea of fire" while proposing national unification.
"How could you regard this as the behaviour of sane people?
"Also, how could you call people sane who loudly talk about building an ideal society for workers and farmers while workers and farmers are starving?"
He explained that he finally decided to abandon his impoverished homeland to "save our people from misfortune" by holding talks with Southern officials.
But Hwang, a leading ideologue, said North Korea was in no danger of collapse. He defended the ruling Worker's Party from which he received "love and consideration".
North Korea says Hwang, one of the architects of Pyongyang's "Juche" philosophy of fanatic self-reliance, must have been kidnapped by Southern authorities.
Separately, a South Korean daily printed a letter purportedly written by Hwang before his flight in which he denounced Pyongyang leader Kim Jong-il.
"The great general's self-admiration has gone so far that he now really believes he is a genius, requiring the people to respect and obey him only."

"How can a society of people, workers, farmers and intelligentsia dying of hunger be called socialist?" the letter said. "In Soviet-style socialism, the dictatorship went too far but there was no hereditary one-man rule."
Kim Jong-il inherited the mantle of leadership from his father, Kim Il-sung, but has yet to formally assume the titles of president and general secretary of the Worker's Party.
The newspaper letter also urged South Korea to beef up its defences against North Korea.

"South Korea must strengthen its fighting forces to defend itself against North Korea which awaits the moment to turn the south into a sea of fire and which tries to dissolve the south internally," it said.
But the main opposition National Congress for New Politics suggested the Chosun Ilbo note, splashed across the newspaper's front page, could be a propaganda ploy by the government.
"Judging from the content, which seems to follow the ruling party line, we think it possible that Hwang may have been guided in writing the letter," said party spokesman Park Hong-yeop.
The newspaper said the letter was delivered to an unnamed South Korean businessman on January 2 by Hwang's aide, Kim Dok-hong, who is also reported to be seeking asylum.
It is not the first time Seoul authorities have been accused of manipulating North Korean defectors.
Last month a controversy flared after two newspapers printed the diary of a teenage boy who defected to South Korea with his family.

The two versions of a dramatic escape across China were similar in content but were written in different hands, leading to suspicions the diary was a hoax perpetrated by South Korean intelligence agents.
